name: asm-dom
workload: Four virtual DOM micro-benchmarks (create 700 nodes, diff 100 times with equal nodes, diff 100 times with different attributes, add/remove 100 children) run in Firefox 67 and Chrome 75, asm-dom (C++ compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten) versus snabbdom.
claimed_speedup: README text says apps written with it 'will run until 4 times faster', but this is a projection, not a measured row. The measured table (lower is better, units unstated) shows Firefox 67: diff equal nodes 2.0 vs 9.0, diff different nodes 20.0 vs 23.0, add/remove 22.0 vs 25.0 (asm-dom ahead), create nodes 1.0 vs 0.0 (asm-dom behind). Chrome 75: diff equal nodes 2.395 vs 3.11 and add/remove 15.17 vs 15.63 (asm-dom ahead), create nodes 0.585 vs 0.455 and diff different nodes 17.795 vs 11.405 (asm-dom behind).
hardware: MacBook Pro (Retina, 13-inch, Late 2013), 2.4 GHz Intel Core i5, 8 GB 1600 MHz DDR3
tradeoffs: Every DOM update still goes through JavaScript, so the JS to WASM binding overhead sits inside the measured path (the README says so itself). Requires Emscripten and writing the whole SPA in C++. asm.js fallback is mentioned in the README. Gains depend on moving application logic into C++, not on the virtual DOM itself.
caveats: Weak and mixed evidence: asm-dom is slower than snabbdom on two of four rows in Chrome and on create nodes in Firefox. The '4 times faster' figure is a stated expectation for whole apps, not a benchmark result. The create-nodes row for asm-dom includes destroying the nodes while snabbdom leaves deletion to the garbage collector, so that row is not like for like. Table units, compiler flags and Emscripten version are not stated. Hardware is from 2013 and browsers are from 2019. Commit date could not be read (the commits page returned 403), so maintenance status is unknown. Kept as a documented flagged entry, not as a clear win.
found_via: Hacker News WebSearch queries (12, over the 10-query limit) returned only wasm-vs-JS discussion threads and no repo; this project was found on the github.com/topics/webassembly?l=c++ listing (2.8k stars) and its benchmark page was opened directly.

name: WebDSP
baseline: its own JavaScript fallback implementations of the same image and video filters (in-browser)
workload: Client-side image and video filters (grayscale, invert, Sobel edge detection, convolution, blur, sharpen) on RGBA canvas pixel data, WebAssembly build versus the JavaScript fallback shipped in the same package.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README states that without WebAssembly support 'the more intensive convolution and edge detection filters will run very slowly or hang the browser completely'.
tradeoffs: Early (2018 era) WebAssembly module loaded by fetch, so it needs an HTTP server; image data must be copied between JS and WASM memory on each call. README TODO notes that several JS fallback filters (underground, rooster, mist, kaleidoscope, bacteria, hulk edge, ghost, twisted) are not yet matched with their C++ versions, so the two paths are not equivalent for those filters.
caveats: Tier D: no benchmark, no numbers, no hardware. Only the qualitative statement above. Included as the single notable D entry (1.5k stars). The baseline is the package's own JS fallback, not an independent JS library and not a native build. Commit date could not be read from the repository page.
found_via: Hacker News WebSearch queries (12, over the 10-query limit) returned only wasm-vs-JS discussion threads and no repo; this project was found on the github.com/topics/webassembly?l=c++ listing (1.5k stars) and its README and repo page were opened directly.
